title: Rule of Law, Judicial Review and the Sunlight of Scrutiny
what_it_is: Rule of Law, Judicial Review and the Sunlight of Scrutiny

sections.label: Judicial review and ouster clauses
sections.summary: CLTPA detention decisions are reviewable in certain respects, but some statutes expressly restrict or exclude judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: For example, it is well established that the Minister's decision to detain a person under the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act or CLTPA, in the interest of public safety, peace and good order is reviewable by the Court in certain respects.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This provides an important safeguard against abuse of power and strengthens the Rule of Law in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: There are, however, a handful of statutes containing provisions that expressly restrict or exclude judicial review.

sections.label: ISA ouster clause and Article 149(3)
sections.summary: Parliament passed legislation introducing the ouster clause into the ISA and introduced Article 149(3) of the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In the result, Parliament not only passed the legislation introducing the ouster clause into the ISA but also introduced Article 149(3) of the Constitution that expressly provides that "nothing in Article 93 shall invalidate" anti-subversion legislation, of which ISA is one.

sections.label: No rebalance for ISA scrutiny
sections.summary: The speaker does not advocate a rebalance in favour of more judicial scrutiny for Executive action under the ISA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Having regard to all these circumstances, I do not advocate a rebalance in favour of more judicial scrutiny for Executive action under the ISA.

sections.label: Employment of Foreign Manpower Act powers
sections.summary: Under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, powers are used against employers for SHN breaches, Fair Consideration Framework breaches and unfair treatment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: For example, today, under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, the Controller of Work Permits and the Minister use the powers not only to determine whether a non-Singaporean should or should not stay in Singapore – which was the focus of the debate in Parliament, when the clause was first enacted – these powers are also used now vis-a-vis additional developments that have arisen in our local context to penalise employers who have failed to discharge their duties to ensure their employees comply with SHN requirements, breached the Fair Consideration Framework, or treated workers unfairly when terminating their services, for example, disguised retrenchment.

sections.label: Reviewing ouster clause rationale
sections.summary: The speaker suggests Parliament consider whether the original rationale behind the ouster clause should extend to new circumstances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I have absolutely no quarrel with the invocation of the powers against such errant employers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: However, given the variety of circumstances in which these powers are currently used, it would be apposite for Parliament to consider whether the original rationale behind the ouster clause should be extended to cover these new circumstances.

sections.label: Court obiter on ouster clause
sections.summary: The Court observed as obiter that excluding jurisdiction even if the Public Prosecutor exceeded his powers would be constitutionally suspect, then found no basis to interfere.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Significantly, however, the Court observed, as obiter, that if the clause was meant to exclude the Court's jurisdiction even if the Public Prosecutor exceeded his limits of power, that provision "would be constitutionally suspect for being in violation of Article 93 as well as the principle of separation of powers." The Court proceeded to review the Public Prosecutor's action and held that there was no basis to interfere with his decision.

sections.label: Review of ouster clauses
sections.summary: The speaker suggests reviewing ouster clauses not dealing with national security, possibly emulating the ISA or CLTPA or amending the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: For statutes containing ouster clauses that do not deal with issues of national security, I would suggest a review.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It may well be that for these statutes, we may have to emulate the approach taken in the ISA or the CLTPA or make relevant amendments to the Constitution to clarify the role of the Judiciary in reviewing the ouster clauses passed by the Legislature and the Executive action in question.

sections.label: Position set out later
sections.summary: The matter requires fuller discussion beyond today's time limit, so their position will be set out substantively on a future occasion.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: They require a fuller discussion, beyond the time limited today under the Standing Orders.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: So, we will set out our position more substantively, on a future occasion.

sections.label: Separation of powers system
sections.summary: The system is based on the separation of powers, with three branches of government each having its own sphere of power and responsibility.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Like many others, our system is based on the separation of powers: three branches of government, each with its own sphere of power and responsibility.

sections.label: Executive and Parliament accountability
sections.summary: The Executive answers to Parliament, and Parliament answers to voters in elections.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In other words, the Executive answers to Parliament, and Parliament answers to voters in elections.

sections.label: Judiciary straying into executive domain
sections.summary: Judges of the Supreme Court have themselves commented that the Judiciary has strayed into the executive domain.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Judges of the Supreme Court have themselves commented that the Judiciary has strayed into the executive domain.

sections.label: Courts balancing government action and safeguards
sections.summary: Singapore Courts have been careful to strike a balance between preserving the Government's ability to act decisively and imposing safeguards against unlawful action.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Singapore Courts have been careful to strike an appropriate balance, between preserving the Government’s ability to act decisively in the public interest, whilst imposing adequate safeguards to check against unlawful action.

sections.label: Courts and Executive judgment
sections.summary: The Courts have repeatedly emphasised that they do not substitute their judgment for that of the Executive and are concerned with the decision-making process, not its merits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: For this reason, the Courts have repeatedly emphasised that they do not substitute their judgment for that of the Executive, and are concerned with the decision-making process, and not its merits.

sections.label: Review of ouster clauses
sections.summary: Mr Pillai asked for a review of ouster clauses; the government will continue to review and calibrate them, and has repealed some, such as former section 14(5) of the Employment Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Mr Pillai has asked for a review of the ouster clauses on our statute books.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We will continue to review the need for such clauses and, where necessary, carefully calibrate these clauses to the intended policy objectives behind such an ouster.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I would add that we have, in fact, on occasion repealed ouster clauses when they are no longer necessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This was the case for the former section 14(5) of the Employment Act.
